comment: Every entry of the server's declared `mcp.limits` must appear here exactly once, and selftest.js fails if the two key sets differ. A limit an agent plans against has to have pinned, observable behaviour at its boundary; one that is declared and never exercised is a claim, not a control.

coverageKinds.boundary: A pair of real sources: one just under the declared value that succeeds, one just over it that fails in the stated way. Run against the live server on every selftest.
coverageKinds.hostGate: Enforced by the adapter before or around execution, so it is exercised through the server's own admission path rather than through a source program.
coverageKinds.injectedLimit: Not reachable at the declared value within `wallTimeMs`, so the boundary is pinned in Rust with a small injected ceiling instead. The `rustTest` field names that test.

sourceBytes.note: Rejected by the adapter on UTF-8 byte length before a backend is entered. The engine applies the same 65536-byte ceiling as `ResourceLimitExceeded { resource: sourceBytes }` if a host ever forwards a larger program.

wallTimeMs.note: The over case was a product of four two-radical sums until the continued-fraction expansion got a work budget. It spent 14s, of which essentially all was *rendering* a 16-term value that took 0.1ms to compute, so it stopped being a wallTimeMs case the moment writing a value down stopped costing seconds; it now answers in 18ms. What replaces it is `UNIQUE`, which is quadratic and priced by nothing: 5k/10k/20k/40k elements take 97ms/388ms/1.86s/7.0s, and at the 100,000-element materialization ceiling it takes about 48s -- ten times over, so the case is decisively over rather than marginally. That it is the best remaining candidate is itself the finding: the work meter prices arithmetic, and the collection Words do real work that no ceiling counts.

responseBytes.note: Both backends measure the same thing: UTF-8 bytes of the schema-1 envelope text. `backend/parity-test.js` runs this pair against both, which is what the native-only `maxBuffer` implementation could never have shown.

concurrentExecutions.note: Exercised through `ExecutionGate` in selftest.js: the gate admits exactly its capacity, queues a further caller for up to CAPACITY_WAIT_MS, hands a released slot to the longest-waiting caller, and answers `capacityExhausted` with `retryable: true` only when the wait elapses.

materializedElements.note: A generative ceiling is a reason-carrying NIL, not an error: the program is well formed and the absence is recoverable with `^`.

numericWork.note: Charged on every rational and algebraic operation in every operand shape, priced as lanes x limb-multiply units, addition included -- Ajisai's `+` is rational addition, three multiplications and a gcd, not anything linear. The pair is a multiquadratic cascade: twelve two-radical factors reach 4,096 terms for about 8.4M units and succeed, the thirteenth doubling costs 16,799,744 and is refused by name. This was `injectedLimit` for three rounds and three different reasons -- arithmetic outside the scalar path was not charged at all, then the refusal's 27MB envelope became `responseTooLarge`, then the twelfth doubling could not be reached because *rendering* 32 terms took 147s. All three are fixed, and the ceiling is observable at its declared value for the first time.

bigintBits.note: Bounds the width of any exact arithmetic result, rational as well as algebraic, in every operand shape. Nineteen multiplications by a 4096-digit literal reach 77,824 digits and succeed; the twentieth would reach 272,133 bits and is refused by name, in about 16ms and 4.2KB of source. The literal is parsed once into a user word, so the pair tests this ceiling rather than `numericLiteralDigits` or the O(n^2) decimal parse. Reaching it costs roughly 9.5M work units, just under `numericWork`'s 10,000,000 -- the two sit close together because building an N-limb integer by multiplication costs about N^2/4 limb-operations by construction, so size and work grow together on this path. Keep that in mind before re-pricing either.

algebraicTerms.note: Reaching 4096 terms is a twelve-factor multiquadratic cascade, and it now computes and renders in about 26ms -- before the continued-fraction expansion got a work budget it was unreachable by eight doublings, because *displaying* 32 terms took 147s. What still hides this ceiling is the one ordering that remains: the thirteenth doubling, which is what would first exceed 4,096 terms, costs 16,799,744 work units against `numericWork`'s 10,000,000, so `numericWork` names itself first. It is a policy question rather than a defect -- a `max_numeric_work` above ~17,000,000 would expose this ceiling at its declared value -- and it is recorded rather than acted on because raising the work an agent program may do is a decision about the host profile, not about the meter.
